evening.title: Get root on a musl Linux system by slamming it with an overly long password
evening.text:
On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions.

The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled.

If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration.

That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not.

Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration.

Dawn of the *sshole

The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually.

In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account.

Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out.

The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk.

Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going.

In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times.

On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack.

Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue, and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set.

There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®

evening.title: October crypto-tracker hack: Access cracked, law enforcement tokens packed
evening.text:
Blockchain analysis outfit Chainalysis has confirmed that when attackers broke into its systems in October, they managed to grab usernames, password hashes, and live tokens.

In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of the attack for the first time.

In previous updates, which Chainalysis has issued regularly since it detected the intrusion on October 30, it confirmed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. The news of password hashes and live tokens also being accessed reflects a worsening picture for the company.

Chainalysis did not confirm the type of hashing algorithm it used to encrypt users' passwords, which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the offline crackability of users' hashed credentials.

Some users received emails instructing them to change their passwords, but Chainalysis said in its latest update that the password reset functionality is currently down. Nevertheless, users were also encouraged to change their passwords on any site where they reuse credentials.

In addition to the exposed data, Chainalysis also detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products, and has taken services down while "our team completes critical work."

These include, but are not limited to, the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page.

Regarding Reactor and the associated investigation data, Chainalysis said: "At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated."

The company plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool at some point today (Thursday November 5).

Customers will have to provide the company’s support team or their account manager with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can begin resetting their passwords.

"We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary.

"We know how business-critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely."

Chainalysis has not yet commented on who was behind the attack, but implied that the culprits used an AI agent, and likened the attack to others that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks."

"This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," it told customers in its initial disclosure on October 30.

"Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems."

In Wednesday's updates, it referred to the intrusion as an "ongoing multifront cyberattack," and later, an "on-path attack," otherwise known as an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) attack, without elaborating further about what it entailed.

Per its own company description, Chainalysis counts government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, financial institutions, and cybersecurity companies among its customer base.

It is one of the world's foremost blockchain analysis companies and is routinely engaged to assist in cyber-related law enforcement investigations.

Recent cases the company was asked to support include the takedowns of crypto-laundering network AudiA6 and bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine, both of which were known facilitators of ransomware crews.

It also played a role in bringing down the infamous LockBit ransomware operation, among other engagements in the interim. ®

evening.title: We Now Know Why Sierra Nevada Corp Canned Its Navy Jet Trainer Bid
evening.text:
The Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) says its decision not to submit a bid to replace the U.S. Navy’s T-45 Goshawk jet trainer was driven by the service’s insistence on a fixed-price contracting structure. The company has also called attention to the potential export opportunities that could emerge for whoever ultimately wins the Undergraduate Jet Training System (UJTS) competition.

For more than a year, SNC had touted plans to compete for UJTS with its Freedom Jet, which was set to be the only clean-sheet design in the running. However, the company confirmed on Tuesday that it had not done so. This has left the Beechcraft M-346N, based on the established M-346 Master jet trainer, submitted by a team made up of U.S. firm Textron and Italy’s Leonardo, as the only known entrant.

Through UJTS, the Navy hopes to acquire 216 new jet trainers to replace its aging fleet of approximately 200 T-45s. The first versions of the Goshawk began entering Navy service in the early 1990s, and the fleet has received significant upgrades since then. The aircraft are aging, and operating and sustaining them have become increasingly challenging. A spate of reported hypoxia-like physiological episodes among pilots led to the development of a new oxygen system in the early 2020s. There have been several Goshawk crashes in recent years due to a variety of factors. The Navy lost another T-45 just in May, with the two individuals onboard thankfully surviving.

SNC had previously said that the Navy’s contracting structure was the central factor behind its decision not to submit a proposal for UJTS, but did not elaborate initially. TWZ reached out for more information and subsequently received a much more detailed response.

Fixed-price risks

“SNC’s decision was driven by the acquisition structure, not the aircraft, the team, or the mission. The current solicitation requires industry to commit to firm-fixed-price production before the aircraft design has fully matured,” SNC told us. “This creates a level of risk we could not responsibly accept and a risk that we believe the Navy will inherit as future cost increases and schedule delays. After careful review, we concluded that we could not commit to pricing a future configuration that has not yet completed the normal design maturation process.”

“Our concerns centered on three related issues: firm-fixed-price production before design maturity, limited visibility into the program’s long-term funding profile, and the requirement to lock in production pricing before key design decisions are finalized,” the company continued in its lengthy statement. “Taken together, those elements place a significant amount of program risk on industry while important aspects of the program are still evolving.”

As the name indicates, firm-fixed-price contracting involves the customer and the vendor agreeing to a hard cost figure up front. Cost growth due to delays and other factors is then generally shouldered by the vendor, though the parties can also renegotiate the terms down the line.

The pros and cons of firm-fixed-price have been a particularly hot topic of debate between the U.S. military and its suppliers for years now. It has been argued that fixed-cost deals are good for U.S. taxpayers, by promoting accountability and preventing an endless stream of funding going into programs that are not delivering results. At the same time, questions have been raised about incentives, or the lack thereof, and the compounding impacts of ballooning costs on program schedules due to factors potentially beyond a company’s control.

Boeing has become something of a poster child for the pitfalls of fixed-price contracting that can emerge on both sides of the equation. In recent years, the company has seen billions of dollars in losses on high-profile fixed-price deals, particularly with the U.S. Air Force. This includes the KC-46 Pegasus aerial refueling tanker and T-7A Red Hawk jet trainer programs. The company has lost more than $3 billion just in the course of work on two new VC-25B Air Force One jets. This is in no small part due to quality control problems and other issues at Boeing. At the same time, fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic and other macroeconomic factors have also played a part.

In April, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that outlined much of this continued debate. It also declared that “it is the policy of my Administration that fixed-price contracts with performance-based considerations should serve as the default and preferred method of procurement in order to advance cost predictability and budget discipline, appropriate contractor incentives and accountability, and streamlined procurement and contract administration.”

Earlier in the year, the Navy had notably announced an increase in the total cost ceiling for the prospective UJTS contract from approximately $1.8 billion to $2.7 billion. At the same time, additional questions have been raised about the availability of funding for the program at the time of the contract award, which is now set to come late next year.

SNC’s clean-sheet Freedom design

SNC had already been taking something of a riskier approach to UJTS. As we noted in the opening of this story, the Freedom jet trainer had been the only clean-sheet design set to compete to replace the Navy’s T-45s. At the time of writing, a prototype has yet to fly. In contrast, the Beechcraft M-346N is based on a design in widespread operational service globally today. Lockheed Martin and Boeing had been expected to put forward versions of existing jet trainers before they dropped out of the running earlier this year.

Furthermore, SNC had been continuing to develop the Freedom jet to be capable of performing carrier qualifications and simulated carrier touch-and-goes at base on land. This is despite the Navy having long ago axed those requirements from the UJTS program as part of a broader shift in how it trains naval aviators. Unlike the service’s current T-45s, the future UJTS jet trainers are not required to be capable of operating from real carriers at all.

Continuing changes to the Navy’s naval aviation training pipelines have been and still are controversial, but it has shown no signs of backtracking. Service officials consistently point to developments in virtualized training and assisted carrier landing capabilities as having fundamentally changed what is required to safely and effectively produce new naval aviators.

“Our decision does not reflect any change in confidence in the Freedom Trainer. Freedom was designed specifically for naval aviation training as a clean-sheet, carrier-capable solution intended to deliver modern training capability and long-term lifecycle savings,” SNC said in response to queries this week. “We continue to believe it is the best option for the Navy’s future jet training needs.”

In statements earlier this week, SNC expressed its willingness to re-engage with the Navy if changes are made to its T-45 replacement plans.

Export potential for any future Navy jet trainer

SNC has also now shared insights into how it previously attempted to address its concerns about the UJTS contracting structure with the Navy. The company notably highlighted potential for export deals facilitated through the U.S. government’s Foreign Military Sales (FMS) program.

“SNC engaged extensively with the Navy on the UJTS requirement over several years and raised these specific concerns directly,” per the company’s statement to us. “We appreciate the professionalism and openness of the Navy and PMA-273 team and have remained engaged in a constructive dialogue throughout the process.”

PMA-273 is the Naval Undergraduate Flight Training Systems Program Office at Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR).

“We have shared several ideas with the Navy, including additional risk-reduction activities through preliminary design review, proposals based on more mature designs and acquisition approaches that better align production commitments with design maturity,” according to SNC. “Greater visibility into the program’s long-term funding profile would also help, with additional pre-planned Foreign Military Sales partnerships developed with and for the joint force training and readiness.”

“Programs at this level should be considering bringing our allied partnership and investment to the table to drive production and affordability on both the front end and the back end,”  SNC’s statement explains. “There are more than 600 FMS trainer aircraft requirements that could be combined in a joint program for the UJTS at a tremendous cost offset to the Department of War”

When Boeing won the Air Force’s T-X competition with what became the T-7A Red Hawk in 2018, TWZ also highlighted the immense potential for foreign sales that could result. Despite interest from several countries for versions of the Red Hawk, no export sales of T-7s have yet been announced. The T-7 program, which is notably being run under a fixed-price contract, has also been beset by technical issues, delays, and cost growth.

How the Navy proceeds now with UJTS, if at all, very much remains to be seen, especially with the M-346N being the only known serious entrant at this point in time.

“The program office is restricted from disclosing this information or commenting on active proposals,” a Navy spokesperson told TWZ when asked for an update on UJTS following SNC’s decision not to bid. “To maintain the integrity of the competitive process, source selection information including bidder identities and proposal details, are restricted from public disclosure.”

It is important to note here that the UJTS program schedule has already slipped multiple times. The original goal was for the Navy to begin receiving new jet trainers in 2028. Now, the initial contract for these jets is not even expected to come until the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027, which runs between July and September of next year.

“I’m unable to share details of the proposal or speculate about the Navy’s next steps,” Textron also told TWZ in a separate statement. “Textron Aviation Defense also brings an established American workforce, supply chain and production capability to support delivery at scale. Combined with a mature Integrated Training System that brings together live, virtual and constructive training, the M-346N offers the U.S. Navy a low-risk solution designed to prepare aviators for the demands of the high-end fight.”

“Ultimately, the Navy is best positioned to determine the path forward, and we stand ready to re-engage if the approach is revisited,” SNC told us. “Our view is simply that robust competition delivers the best value for the Navy and the taxpayer over a program of this duration. We would welcome the opportunity to compete under a structure that we can responsibly support.”

For now, as far as we know, the Navy is pushing ahead with UJTS, even though there appears to be only one contender for the fixed-price contract.

evening.title: openSUSE Leap 16.1 gives Linux users the right to remain immutable
evening.text:
openSUSE Leap 16.1 lets users choose between a conventional Linux installation and an immutable system from the same installer, bringing the previously separate Leap Micro into the fold.

It's the first point release after Leap 16.0, which we looked at last year when it reached the release candidate stage.

Leap 16.1 has arrived ahead of its paid enterprise sibling, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.1, which is expected later this month. Its release notes are already available, and IBM discussed the release in September.

The big change in the 16.1 release cycle of both the free and commercial products is that SUSE is merging its conventional Linux with its immutable version, a change the company announced back in February.

SUSE previously offered a commercial stripped-down immutable OS, aimed mainly at hosting containers, called SLE Micro. To correspond with that, there was a free community OS called Leap Micro – the final release was Leap Micro 6.2.

Leap Micro is being discontinued as a separate community distribution. The Leap 16.1 announcement says: "Immutable Mode with transactionally updating a system with a read-only root filesystem is a big change for this release. Users who know Leap Micro will recognize it right away, because it is the same approach, now integrated directly into Leap. Leap 16.1 in Immutable Mode replaces Leap Micro, and there will be no Leap Micro 6.3 or 7.0. Users simply boot the regular Leap 16.1 install image and select Immutable Mode in Agama."

Both Red Hat and Canonical offer immutable distros, but both use different architectures from their conventional package-based distros. Ubuntu Core is built entirely from snap packages, while Red Hat's "Atomic" immutable distros are built from bootable containers, running on top of OStree, which works a little like a local Git server. Immutable distros built on Arch, such as SteamOS 3 or KDE Linux, resemble ChromeOS at filesystem level, with dual root filesystems that update one another.

Leap belongs to the openSUSE family of distros, backed by enterprise Linux vendor SUSE. Its commercial sibling is SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES). Leap is the free, community-supported version, and they are based on the same core packages and release schedule. openSUSE also has a rolling-release version, called Tumbleweed.

To rephrase this in terms of slightly more familiar Red Hat equivalents, SLES is SUSE's equivalent of RHEL. Leap is the free openSUSE equivalent of the late lamented CentOS Linux. Leap shares a common core with SUSE's enterprise products while offering a broader community package selection. SLES and openSUSE began sharing enterprise binaries in 2021. Red Hat, meanwhile, announced the end of CentOS Linux in 2020, shifting its focus to CentOS Stream.

To continue the Red Hat comparisons, openSUSE Tumbleweed is loosely equivalent to Fedora Rawhide, but with automated testing and rollback of problematic updates. Unlike the best-known rolling distro, the entirely community-built Arch Linux, Tumbleweed uses SUSE's Snapper technology to offer snapshots. If an update breaks something, Tumbleweed users can boot into a snapshot of an older version of the OS, before the offending update was installed, and keep on working. If dozens of updated packages a day prove too much, then openSUSE also offers an experimental slower-moving rolling release called Slowroll.

Despite the modest version-number bump, Leap 16.1 is a substantial annual update. Its release cycle sits between Fedora and interim Ubuntu releases on one side, and Debian and Ubuntu LTS on the other. Along with its other updates, it brings GNOME 48.8, KDE Plasma 6.6.4, and LXQt 2.4.

We tried its Xfce desktop, which surprisingly defaulted to X.org rather than the Wayland-based setup using labwc that we saw in 16.0 last year.

Immutable distros look to be the future of Linux for non-technical users. Android is an immutable OS based on the Linux kernel, and sells in the billions – which is why, as we reported last year, Google is replacing ChromeOS with Android. The result is the AI-festooned GooglebookOS, on sale in Mountain View's new high-end GoogleBook kit.

The Reg FOSS desk isn't aware of any other Linux OS in which you're able to choose, at the point of installation, whether you wish it to be immutable or not. For now, in the commercial Linux OS space, only SUSE has anything like this flexibility. It's marketing its immutable versions as being ideal hosts for containers, and as suitable for "edge" devices, meaning that they are expected to be provisioned remotely, update themselves automatically, and recover from faults on their own.

SUSE is a much smaller company than Red Hat, and unfortunately, as we reported earlier this week, it is getting smaller.

This vulture is both a former SUSE Linux user and a former SUSE employee, and we hope it and its unique distribution survive and thrive. ®

evening.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber, and promises this one stays within 'rules of engagement'
evening.text:
OpenAI, on Thursday, released its latest cybersecurity-tuned model, GPT-6 Cyber, which the House of Altman says combines "stronger cybersecurity capabilities with better adherence to researchers’ rules of engagement."

The new model, we’re told, is much better at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, compared to GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra.

OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra in early September, and less than a month later, killed off the planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra after the model got better at pursuing tasks but worse at staying within the boundaries of what it had actually been authorized to do.

The model maker said the latest cyber model was "trained to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions and report results accurately."

In OpenAI's ExploitGym training evaluation, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent. For comparison, GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1 percent on these same benchmark tests.

"In a separate evaluation of whether the model respects the boundaries of an assigned task, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services over 99 percent of the time," Open AI said. Only 0.07 percent of cases went beyond the intended scope of the training exercise.

OpenAI declined to provide additional details about what happened in that 0.07 percent of cases and whether they involved any real-life safety or security incidents - like hacking companies or carrying out supply chain attacks as its earlier models have done during training. We do know, however, that OpenAI recently began denying internet access to the frontier models it is training to help prevent its models from doing bad things.

The latest cyber model is also really good at finding and exploiting serious security vulnerabilities, OpenAI claimed. Its researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, which Mozilla has started fixing. The model also helped researchers develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown bugs. The Linux findings are being reported with potential patches for maintainer review.

OpenAI classified GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” under its Preparedness Framework. This is its highest-risk tier for cyber capabilities, and means a model can both identify and develop functional zero-day exploits in real-world critical systems, and execute end-to-end cyberattacks.

As such, it’s initially only available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers - these are customers who are authorized to use OpenAI’s models for offensive security actions such as proof-of-concept exploit development, exploit-chain validation, penetration testing, and red teaming.

Over the coming weeks, OpenAI will expand access to all Daybreak Red customers, and is also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to this group, as well.

The model release comes as OpenAI makes a concerted push to improve the security of its products.

Earlier this week, OpenAI raised its bug bounty reward payments, and added new bonuses for independent researchers.

This includes quadrupling reward-range midpoints, on average, for medium, high and critical findings, so a critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000 - or up to or $51,577 after bonuses - compared to the previous $6,500 payout.

Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses.®

evening.title: Copilot Chat has usage caps, and Microsoft would rather you found them by hitting them
evening.text:
Microsoft is applying usage limits to more Copilot Chat features for commercial users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, and it won't publish the numerical caps.

Copilot Chat comes with qualifying Microsoft 365 business and enterprise subscriptions. Without the Copilot add-on, it can reason over web information and uploaded files. The paid license adds broader access to work data, including emails, meetings, chats, and documents.

Tasks already in progress won't be interrupted. Once a limit is reached, users will receive an in-product notice explaining when to retry the affected feature.

Administrators can't adjust these limits; Microsoft sets them. The Windows behemoth says it "doesn't publish specific limits because they're subject to change."

Microsoft also suggests that hitting a limit "might indicate interest in additional Copilot capabilities." The remedy it proposes for administrators to consider is, conveniently, another license.

Users may also be offered an upgrade route – although buying a license themselves depends on whether their organization permits self-service purchases. Microsoft explained: "In most organizations, the limit notification includes an option to upgrade.

"Users can select it to request a Microsoft 365 Copilot license from their admin, who can approve or deny requests in the Microsoft 365 admin center. If the organization allows users to buy licenses directly, users might also see an option to purchase a license."

Microsoft concluded: "Admins can turn off direct purchases for each product."

The rollout began on November 2 for organizations with 2,000 or fewer Microsoft 365 seats and is due to start on November 9 for larger organizations. It also applies only to users without a Microsoft 365 Copilot license in commercial tenants. Web, desktop, and mobile apps are all affected.

The change could be Microsoft's latest wheeze to turn included Copilot Chat access into paid add-on sales. Users who hit an unpublished ceiling may well start pestering administrators for an upgrade.

The alternative is that admins decide tighter controls are preferable to unpredictable feature availability. Not necessarily the sales outcome Microsoft had in mind. ®

evening.title: Two Soldiers Killed After Military Vehicle Meets With Accident in Ladakh
evening.text:
Two soldiers were killed on Wednesday in a road accident in the Namika La Pass area on the Kargil-Leh National Highway.
Officials said two Indian Army personnel, the driver and co-driver, were killed when their heavy-duty military vehicle skidded off the road and plunged into a deep gorge near Namika La Pass on National Highway-01 (Kargil-Leh National Highway) in Ladakh.
Officials said the accident occurred at approximately 1.30 pm near Namika La Pass in the Kargil-Leh sector.
Both soldiers on board died on the spot. Local police and rescue teams recovered the bodies and shifted them to the Community Health Centre (CHC) in Chiktan for medico-legal formalities and postmortem examinations.
“A case has been registered at Police Station Wakha under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), and an investigation into the cause of the accident is underway,” officials said.
Namika La Pass, also known as the ‘Pillar of the Sky Pass’, is a high mountain pass at 3,700 metres (12,139 feet) above sea level in the Zanskar Range of Ladakh.
It is situated along the Srinagar-Leh Highway (NH-1), roughly 105 km from Leh and 54 km from Kargil. It is one of two major high passes between Kargil and Leh, paired with the higher Fotu La Pass.
Translated locally, Namika La Pass is called the ‘Pillar of the Sky’.
Indian Army operates under some of the most extreme climatic and geographical conditions in the World. The army secures crucial front lines including the Line of Actual Control (LAC) facing China and the Line of Control (LoC) facing Pakistan.
Troops are deployed across high-altitude plains, deep valleys, and rugged mountain passes ranging from 3,000 metres to over 6,000 metres above sea level.
At Siachen Glacier, known as the World’s highest battlefield, soldiers hold positions at altitudes exceeding 5,400 metres (18,000 feet), where temperatures routinely plummet below -40°C.
In Eastern Ladakh & Pangong Tso, following heightened security requirements in recent years, the Army maintains significant forward deployments across the Ladakh plateau, including the shores of the strategic Pangong Lake and the Galwan Valley.
Source: IANS

Tobacco company got smoked by leaving secret recipes on a file share
evening.text:
Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture.

Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets.

Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it.

"I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here."

Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client.

"My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes."

Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company.

He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside.

The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share."

“I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file.

Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated.

But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all.

He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all.

"And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe."

He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it.

"The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®

evening.title: RTsys Group Strengthens Its Presence in Canada with the Sale of Several SEMA Training Targets
evening.text:
At Euronaval 2026, the Morbihan-based RTsys Group announced the sale of several SEMA training targets to two Canadian defense agencies: Defense Research and Development Canada (DRDC) and the Naval Engineering Test Establishment (NETE). This marks a new international milestone for its anti-submarine warfare (ASW) solution, further solidifying its presence in the North American naval defense market. 

RTsys press release

Developed by RTsys Underwater Technologies, a subsidiary of the group, SEMA is a recoverable acoustic target designed to train naval forces in anti-submarine warfare (ASW). It simulates the presence of a submarine, trains operators in its detection and tracking, and enables torpedo-firing exercises without deploying an actual submarine. The solution is notably compatible with modern sonars and the latest-generation torpedoes. 

Unveiled at Euronaval 2026, the third-generation target, SEMA MK-III, marks a new technological milestone. In particular, it incorporates the ability to simulate a submarine’s magnetic signature, in addition to its acoustic signature. Equipped with an Iridium satellite link and now recoverable by helicopter winch, it expands training capabilities, particularly for missions conducted from helicopters. New software also facilitates mission planning and monitoring. 

“This new collaboration with Canadian organizations confirms the recognition of our solutions among international naval defense stakeholders. It demonstrates our ability to evolve our technologies to meet the operational needs of armed forces and to develop lasting international partnerships,” says François-Xavier de Cointet, CEO of RTsys Group. 

As a supplier to several NATO navies in North America, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region, RTsys Group is continuing to expand its presence in the submarine defense market. 

The group will be exhibiting at Euronaval 2026, November 3–6 at Paris Nord Villepinte (Hall 6, Booth F99), where it will also showcase two other new products: SONADIVE MK-II and SONABLOW.

evening.text:
The Union Cabinet’s decision to offer two-year additional tenure to the ‘Agniveers’, beyond their stipulated four-year service, has been welcomed by a couple of Defence Experts as they foresee it as a “mutually beneficial” step going forward.
“This will prove to be mutually beneficial for both the Armed Forces as well as Agniveers, as the latter, having trained in multi-pronged operations over a period of time, will enrich the services,” said Defence Expert Brig. Hemant Mahajan (Retd) speaking to IANS.

He said that the changes in the Agnipath scheme will also enhance chances of their (Agniveers) absorption into the forces.
Dhruv Katoch, a noted defence expert, also welcomed the move as the early onset of Diwali for the Agniveers.
“I consider this a very positive step, and I would say that Diwali has arrived four days early for all the Agniveers,” Katoch remarked.
The Agnipath scheme, rolled out in June 2022, entailed recruitment of soldiers for a four-year term, with a provision to retain 25 per cent of them in regular services.
Bringing a major change in the recruitment process, also seen as a rollback in the policy, the government on Wednesday announced that Agniveers, after the end of their four-year tenure, will get an additional two-year extension period and will also be offered permanent recruitment, subject to meeting specific eligibility criteria and individual consent.
The move comes weeks before the three services were to start releasing 75% of Agniveers from their first batch in a phased manner starting mid-November. Over 18,300 Agniveers are set to exit the Armed Forces by December 31 after completing a four-year term.

evening.title: IAF C-17 Paint Peeling Is Not Necessarily a Safety Issue
evening.text:
An Indian Air Force C-17 Globemaster III has come under the spotlight following the circulation of photographs showing significant paint peeling on the forward fuselage. The aircraft’s appearance has naturally led to some speculation about its state, though the extent of the paint delamination visible is in itself nothing to be concerned about in terms of structural integrity or aircraft safety.
Paint delamination is the loss of adhesion of the paint to the underlying surface. Aircraft operating in the field are subject to UV radiation, temperature variation, moisture, fuel and hydraulic fluid contamination, cleaning agents and a whole host of maintenance activities. All of these can contribute to the degradation of the paint system over time.
With respect to the C-17 in the photos, sections of the external topcoat appear to have delaminated from the underlying coat. The areas that have come away could be primer or another layer of the aircraft’s protective coating system. A photo however doesn’t prove which layer has come away or whether the underlying protective system is still there.
Aircraft exterior paint is not a structural component at all. The strength of the airframe comes from the metal and composites of the structure itself, not the paint. Localised paint loss therefore doesn’t in any way mean that the aircraft has sustained any structural damage or that it’s unsafe to fly.
Aircraft coatings have a purpose beyond just looking good. They’re there to protect the airframe underneath from the effects of the environment and from corrosion. If delamination has exposed the primer or the bare substrate then the maintenance people have to assess the degree of coating failure and decide whether or not corrosion prevention or restoration work is required.
In those circumstances the aircraft operator’s maintenance team would normally carry out an assessment of the affected area in line with the manufacturer’s maintenance manual. That assessment would determine whether the damage is confined to the topcoat, whether the primer is still there and whether there is any sign of corrosion, surface deterioration or damage to the substrate.
Depending on the findings the maintenance required could be as simple as local surface prep and repaint or could be as extensive as full coating restoration with corrosion control. The aircraft manufacturer would of course be consulted where appropriate in accordance with the applicable maintenance procedures.
The C-17 is built to operate in very demanding environments, in and around which its external surfaces will be subject to a great deal of wear. Paint deterioration is therefore a maintenance issue that has to be dealt with over the life of the aircraft.

Memory makers mint megabucks while buyers beg for mercy
evening.text:
The big memory manufacturers continue to print money at the expense of long-suffering buyers, with industry DRAM revenue approaching five times its level a year ago.

Demand for datacenter capacity and AI accelerators drove the 369 percent year-over-year surge in Q3 2026, Counterpoint Research reports.

"Bit shipments rose only about 4 percent this quarter, yet DRAM revenue reached nearly $200 billion, close to 5x a year ago," says Counterpoint senior analyst Jeongku Choi.

"AI has turned memory from a commodity into a valuable scarce resource, and buyers are now competing for supply rather than negotiating on price. With prices still rising, suppliers are on track to set new earnings records again next quarter."

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, the AI infrastructure boom has sent demand for server memory soaring. Manufacturers have prioritized more lucrative products for that market, squeezing supplies for PCs, smartphones, and other devices.

The consequences have been a sharp increase in memory costs, leading to higher prices of products that use it. The average price tag for a laptop or desktop was up by double-digit percentages across Europe this summer, resulting in falling PC shipments as vendors struggled to secure supplies and buyers were put off by the expense.

A similar effect has been seen in the smartphone arena, with shipments down by at least a fifth as rising memory costs squeezed budget models out of the market, leaving vendors to focus on high-end devices instead.

Price increases slowed from the steep rises seen in the first half of the year, Counterpoint says, but average DRAM selling prices still reached $1.90 per gigabit and remained the main driver of revenue growth.

Of the big three memory makers – the DRAMvirate, if you like – Samsung led with a 38 percent share of DRAM revenue. Separately, it forecast company-wide operating profit of about $80 billion for Q3, up from $9 billion a year earlier.

SK hynix posted stronger sequential growth, helping it recover some of the share it lost earlier this year, according to Counterpoint. The firm made a $62.8 billion profit, and predicts that memory shortages will persist until at least 2030.

Micron's DRAM revenue grew more slowly than rivals', but its wider business hardly suffered: fiscal fourth-quarter net profit reached $37.7 billion, exceeding its entire second-quarter revenue of $23.8 billion.

Counterpoint's research director MS Hwang expects to see memory prices remaining high next year.

"[High-bandwidth memory] prices, which lagged commodity DRAM this year, are now catching up. Long-term agreements (LTAs) are supporting prices, and supply will stay tight because major new fabs will not start production until 2028. LTA terms may cause results to differ between suppliers in the short term, but over time they should all follow the same upward trend," he says.

That means more bad news for buyers, but more massive profits for the memory makers. ®

Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains.

Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through our supply chains is just a fascinating way of making sense of the global economy. It feels like the only thing the system isn’t resilient to is the AI industry wanting every scrap of RAM that the whole world can produce. And so now there’s not going to be inexpensive cell phones.

What will push the system over the breaking point? Because globalization has seemed generally resilient to a bunch of people who want it to be over.

I think what you’re highlighting is that it’s really the power of the market. In the case of closing the Strait of Hormuz, Brent North Sea crude prices didn’t go to $150 a barrel like I was afraid they would, and a lot of people were afraid they would because the market adjusted.

We applied a lot of tariffs on Liberation Day. The first response was circumvention or front-running. The next response was tariff engineering. The next response is like, “Okay, let me move production to Vietnam or let me move production to Mexico, and I’ll find a way around that.” Now, eventually, when you close down all those things, then prices eventually have to rise.

In the case of memory chips, that’s a different problem because the demand far outstripped the capacity. I used to always buy memory cards on Black Friday. Forget that this year.

Yeah, it’s all over.

I’m just glad I stocked up on a previous Black Friday.

If you want to know my prediction for when the AI industry will meet its true political end, it’s when Grand Theft Auto VI comes out. Everyone goes out to buy a PS5, and they realize it’s more expensive now at the end of its life cycle than it was at the beginning because the price of memory has skyrocketed.

Yeah, no kidding. We’re talking about huge amounts. But that’s the same thing. We’re in a phase where we see all these tactical actions taken by the government, very transactional, without necessarily understanding all the complex interconnections and interdependencies.

You may have noticed, for example, that the administration temporarily suspended the Jones Act. I don’t know if you remember that. Why did they temporarily suspend the Jones Act? Because oil refineries on the East Coast of the US couldn’t get their oil from Texas cheaply because there were no domestic supertankers.

The Jones Act requires that if you move stuff from Texas to New Jersey, you have to have a US-owned, US-crewed, US-built, very large crude carrier. There aren’t any because we don’t build those in the US. So that’s why it’s cheaper to bring oil from Algeria to New Jersey than it is to bring it from Texas. And that’s why they suspended the Jones Act for a while. At least they understood that.

I know at least some of our audience is going to be listening to this conversation, and you’re steeped in global trade. You wrote a book to educate our government about how it works from the basics, which I think is sorely needed.

But a lot of the promise for young people in our politics lately is that we will rebuild American capacity. We will rebuild manufacturing capacity. We will bring back a bunch of jobs where you don’t need an advanced degree in AI prompt engineering or whatever to see the future. We will bring back the dignity of work.

Politicians on both sides are making these promises all the time, and a lot of that requires closing down trade, forcing that economic activity back within our borders. It just seems like that isn’t likely. So I’m not going to ask you whether or not that is totally likely. I’m going to ask: what’s more likely instead?

Well, I think what’s more likely is that we will see efforts as you describe. I would love to sit down with people and say, okay, we want to move this type of production back to the US. Let’s take a more strategic, more nuanced approach, understanding the bigger picture, considering what levers are available.

The US is still a big, attractive market. It is the largest market in the world. It is the most attractive market in the world. That’s, by the way, why the Chinese all want to come here: because they can make some money here that they can’t make elsewhere. So then how do we harness that market power and that market pull with a more nuanced understanding of why our supply chains are organized the way they are today? Recognizing that, can I build a strategy to bring important things that are very strategic for the US to know how to do?

Let’s think about how we fix this problem with an understanding of that bigger picture.

Willy, it’s been great to talk to you. It is always just a pleasure. We have to have you back faster than five years. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.

Thanks for having me.

evening.title: Microsoft fixed Excel 2016 copy-paste bug. Then reintroduced it. Now it's fixed again
evening.text:
The Excel copy-and-paste bug is back, which means Microsoft is making a second round of fixes.

The bug first appeared in the September update and manifested in multiple versions of Excel as a silent failure of the paste operation. Users copied content and attempted to paste it, but the destination cell was unchanged no matter how hard they mashed the Ctrl+V keys. Microsoft fixed it in mid-September. But it made a comeback in Excel 2016 when users installed October's security update.

Microsoft has now released a new build of Excel 2016 to address the reintroduction of the bug: build 16.0.5574.1006. The company wrote: "The new build includes all security updates for Microsoft Excel 2016, and also fixes the issue that was reintroduced in 16.0.5574.1005, in which paste operations might fail if the workbook contains conditional formatting."

Microsoft did not explain how the bug slipped back in. Copy and paste is, after all, a niche bit of functionality.

Users reported the recurrence of the bug in October after the KB5002934 update was applied. Rolling back the update resolved the problem until Windows Update pushed the patch again. KB5002934 is a security update that resolves glitches including remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities.

The problem affects only Excel 2016 and is not the result of the latest Windows security update. Rather, it was reintroduced in an Excel update delivered through Windows Update. A user in a Microsoft Excel forum said the issue had appeared on workstations throughout their organization. "What's frustrating is that this is the same issue we encountered before, which was supposedly fixed in a previous update. Now it's back, barely a few weeks later."

And now, at least, it appears to be fixed once again. Still, if Microsoft is determined to reintroduce bugs into Excel, perhaps it might also be tempted to bring back the Hall of Tortured Souls (a secret first-person 3D mini-game hidden inside Microsoft Excel for Windows 95) and populate it with the testers who managed to miss the issue's resurrection. ®

'Stop dirty datacenters': Europe-wide protests planned demanding building moratorium
evening.text:
Campaigners against datacenter expansion are planning two days of coordinated action across Europe on November 6 and 7, demanding an immediate moratorium on new large-scale developments.

Following the US midterm elections, where restrictions on massive AI server farms were prominent in the campaigns from candidates in both major parties, it's now Europe's turn. Over 100 groups across 15 European countries will protest the boom in bit barn building over the next couple of days.

As well as demonstrations, there will be public meetings, stalls, petitions, walking tours, cycle rides, poetry readings and other creative actions, the organizers say.

The coalition of groups has put up a website – stopdirtydatacentres.eu – with an interactive map allowing anyone to find information on the events taking place and where.

In the UK, there is a photocall planned at 8am on November 6 outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) in Whitehall Place in central London, but also a Community Day of Action the following day at London's Brick Lane, where a facility is planned on the site of the former Truman Brewery.

Also on November 7, there will be a "family event" at St Michaels & All Angels Church in Great Torrington, Devon, to highlight the massive 1.5 GW data campus and on-site battery energy storage that is planned for 850 acres of farmland near the town.

The planned actions are a response to growing concerns about the impact of the wave of new compute shed projects on local communities, public infrastructure, land, water and energy use, housing, jobs and the cost of living.

Such concerns won't have been helped by recent events, such as a Google subsidiary reportedly felling 250,000 trees illegally in Finland to clear the ground for a server hall.

The campaigners claim that governments, the European Union and the tech giants are gambling with the future by racing ahead with server farm developments without proper scrutiny of the environmental, democratic and social impacts they might have.

A recent report found that businesses and private-sector trade associations dominated meetings with UK ministers to discuss datacenters, while environmental groups didn't get a look-in.

Campaigners are calling for an immediate moratorium on new large-scale projects across Europe, until clear frameworks are in place to determine whether new facilities should be built and under what conditions, with proper scrutiny and meaningful public participation.

"Datacenter developers in the UK and Europe want to cash in on the AI goldrush whatever the consequences. But communities everywhere are fighting back, seeing through Big Tech's PR machine and calling this what it is – a massive grab of scarce land, water and power resources by Silicon Valley billionaires," said Oliver Hayes, Head of Campaigns at Global Action Plan (UK).

"With governments failing to answer very basic questions about how many datacenters we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided, the only reasonable course of action is an immediate moratorium," he said in a supplied remark.

They are unlikely to get much sympathy from the British government, which has pegged its hopes for economic growth on AI and wants more bit barns built to fulfil this. It has already used its powers to overturn rejections of planning permission for server farm projects by local councils.

Omdia analyst Alan Howard argues that datacenters also became a convenient political target during the US campaigns.

"The datacenter industry took a big hit in the US midterm elections which is quite disappointing, but not that surprising," Howard told The Register.

"The anti-datacenter rhetoric accelerated 12 months ago and in the last six months skyrocketed. While there have been many catalysts to point our fingers at, datacenters turned into an opportunistic political football. To be blunt, there is no shortage of politicians willing to exploit any opportunity to win an election and the datacenter 'problem' showed up just at the right time for this election."

Planned actions across Europe include events in Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, the Netherlands, France, and the UK. A march to the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh is also pegged for the following weekend, November 14. ®

Did PL-15 Jamming Concerns Push Pakistan Towards IIR Guided Fa’az Missile Technology?
evening.text:
Pakistan has flight tested its FAAZ air-to-air missile and thus has introduced a new indigenous weapon into the PAF’s BVR missile programme. The ISPR statement on the matter didn’t provide any details on the missile’s specs, though the missile in question is of interest given that GIDS (the developer) has previously demonstrated both a radar guided and an IIR (imaging infrared) version of the missile with claimed ranges in excess of 100km.
The test (announced on 3rd November) is the first publicly confirmed flight test of the FAAZ missile. Pakistan has released footage of the missile being launched from a JF-17. The ISPR has described it as an indigenously developed air-to-air missile with an advanced terminal guidance system, capable of engaging aerial targets at longer ranges.
However the military didn’t identify the seeker fitted to the missile that was tested nor did they reveal the type of target or the engagement conditions.
FAAZ is not a brand new programme. Two variants were publicly demonstrated by GIDS at the IDEF defence exhibition in Türkiye in July 2023: FAAZ-RF (with an active radar seeker) and FAAZ-IIR (with an imaging infra red seeker).
As per the information provided by GIDS at the show, both variants were advertised with ranges in excess of 100 km and a max speed of Mach 3.5. GIDS also cited a seeker detection range of 25 km for the radar version and 40 km for the IIR version. At the time GIDS CEO Asad Kamal was quoted in Defence News as confirming to Defence News that the missiles on display were in fact mock-ups.The IIR option is of particular interest in that it represents a different approach to terminal guidance. Rather than an active radar seeker which uses radar energy to home in on and track the target, the IIR uses the target’s heat signature to guide the missile in the terminal phase.
This can make an IR guided missile less prone to conventional radar jamming. It doesn’t make it immune to all forms of countermeasures though. Aircraft can still use flares, manoeuvres and all the other tricks of the trade to break up the IR tracking. The effectiveness of an IIR missile is also very much dependent on the aspect of the target, the weather, the range at which it’s detected and the quality of the seeker. A closer look at the FAAZ airframe suggests it’s very similar to the Chinese SD-10 (the export version of the PL-12 BVRAAM). The general shape and aerodynamic layout are very much in keeping with that of the Chinese missile, though there is no public confirmation that the FAAZ is in fact a derivative of the Chinese weapon.
The PL-12 has a history of reported Russian technical assistance. The US Air University’s China Aerospace Studies Institute has referenced Russian involvement in the programme, including technical assistance from missile manufacturers and the use of an Agat developed seeker (which is associated with Vympel’s R-77 family of missiles).
The PL-12 is a dual thrust solid propellant rocket motor with active radar homing. It’s bigger than the American AIM-120 AMRAAM, which is in itself a rather telling indicator of the different approach taken to range and missile performance.
Whether FAAZ has retained any of the PL-12’s propulsion or guidance architecture is not known. GIDS have presented the missile as a system developed locally but the degree of foreign design influence has not been made public.
The prospect of a 100km class IIR guided AAM would give Pakistan another guidance option in addition to their conventional radar homing weapons. It would be a useful asset in the event that the adversary is employing EW systems to jam the radar homing seekers.
This is of course relevant to the wider discussion around long range air combat post Operation Sindoor. The IAF were able to slip past the PL-15E missiles that Pakistan launched during the 2025 encounter by successfully jamming them and a number of the missiles were recovered in various locations. It appears that for a country which already has the RF variant of the PL-15 and also has the longer range PL-15 at its disposal, the decision to go with the FAAZ-IIR is a very direct response to the PL-15E’s proven failure.
India already has infrared guided MICA missiles on its Rafale and Mirage 2000 fleets. The MICA family is available in both radar and imaging infrared seeker variants so the same missile family can be used to meet a range of different engagement requirements. India also has ASRAAM on its Jaguar aircraft and that was the weapon selected for the Tejas Mk1A programme.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: Joint Ventures May Deny India Critical Engine IP, Warns GTRE
evening.text:
The risks involved in various models of international cooperation in developing advanced fighter engines were explained by Dr S.V. Ramana Murty, Director of the Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE). He explained that a traditional joint venture model may not ensure IP ownership and full technology transfer from the foreign partner.
Speaking during the third Delhi Defence Dialogue organised by the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA), Murty spoke about the options available to India to develop advanced military aircraft propulsion systems. This includes co-design and co-development with an foreign engine manufacturer, indigenous development, a joint venture or a multinational consortium such as the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) or Future Combat Air System (FCAS).
He highlighted the importance of technology availability, IP ownership, time to develop and investment.
Options for developing an advanced fighter engine
Option 1: Co-design and co-development with a foreign engine manufacturer. This will allow access to mature engineering skills but provides opportunities for involvement in the design and development process for Indian organisations.
Option 2: Indigenous development. While this would involve many design cycles and take a long time to develop, this option would carry a medium risk and cost. However, this would provide more opportunities to keep control of the technology developed.
Option 3: Joint venture. This was seen as being a higher risk. Traditional joint venture agreements may not provide the right level of technology availability needed to develop its own national capability.
This may result in limited know-how and know-why shared between the partners, meaning that IP may still be owned by the foreign organisation. This creates a high risk scenario where India may be reliant on its partners.
Option 4: Multinational consortium such as GCAP/FCAS. This brings multiple countries together but will require large investments and long term planning.
Six requirements to look for when looking to partner internationally:
Full know-how and know-why must be shared within their portion of work. Shared IP ownership. Performance guarantee. Unrestricted technology availability. Willingness to export. Production in India.
Shared IP and unrestricted technology is very important. If manufacturing is done with an Indian company to assemble or manufacture certain components of the engine, there is no guarantee that they are able to modify, upgrade or manufacture the whole engine themselves.

Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States.

The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor.

“When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. evening.title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
evening.text:
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years. 

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.  

The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.

So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)

One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.

The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.

Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.

Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.

A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.

Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.

But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.

“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.

This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change. 

In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.

Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.
evening.summary: A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

evening.title: Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupe first drive: Where tech and fun collide
evening.text:
Mercedes-Benz provided flights from San Francisco to Malaga, Spain, and accommodation so Ars could drive the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe. Ars does not accept paid editorial content.

The night before I drove the AMG GT 4-Door Coupe, I complained to a group of journalists that automakers don't want to take chances and just build fun, weird cars anymore. About 12 hours later, Mercedes made me eat my words. Outside of all the bombastic extravaganza of the Los Angeles launch, the first true AMG powered exclusively by batteries is a technological triumph that's as comfortable on the track as it is on the street. And it's really very good on the track.

Triforce

One of the fundamental problems with EVs is weight. Batteries are heavy, and the old rule about an object in motion tending to stay in motion makes the notion of nimble cornering a difficult engineering problem. Mercedes loves an engineering problem, and after two days behind the wheel of the AMG GT EV, the company has mostly reduced the battery-weight tax that mires EV performance.

On the road and on the track, the vehicle is firmly planted to the roadway. Mercedes says various technologies make this possible. In addition to decades of producing high-performance vehicles, the automaker's AMG.EA sports-car architecture does a lot of heavy lifting here, constantly adjusting power delivery from the three motors while guiding the Active Ride Control suspension, steering—including up to 6 degrees at the rear axle—and active aerodynamics to deliver the performance AMG customers have come to expect from a vehicle with the Affalterbach badge on the hood.
